title: Second Declension Nouns
objectives: understand the English syntax of nouns in sentences (subject, object, number, gender, etc.)
understand the Greek noun system (gender, number, case)
write out the second declension paradigm for masculine and neuter nouns
master 10 more high frequency vocabulary words
_objectives_note: Extracted verbatim from 0x09415c. A near duplicate at 0x0b7706 drops "the" in line 1; that is a stale buffer, not the page.

content.text: A noun is commonly defined as a word that stands for a person, place or thing.

Gender in English is determined by the sex of the referent:  "king...he", "queen...she".  Objects which are neither male nor female are considered neuter:  "table...it".  In Greek some inanimate objects are given male or female designations.  Be careful not to confuse Greek grammatical gender with biological gender.
Both English and Greek inflect words for number.   Both languages have singular and plural nouns.
English uses three word inflections in order to indicate changes in case.
The subject of the sentence can usually be discovered by putting "who" or "what" before the verb.
E.g.   [[u]]Zach[[/u]] ran to the store.
Who ran to the store?    Zach (= subject)
The object of a sentence can usually be discovered by putting a "who" or "what" after the verb.
E.g.   Zach hit [[u]]the ball[[/u]].
Zach hit what?    ball (= object)
The possessive case often can be discovered by asking "whose"?
Charlie hid [[u]]his[[/u]] ball.
whose ball?    his (possessive)

There are three noun [[u]][[link:declensions]]declensions[[/link]][[/u]] in Greek.  We will learn the second declension first because it is more frequent.  Second declension nouns are largely masculine which is indicated by placing a " ὁ  " [[u]][[link:definiteArticle]]definite article[[/link]][[/u]] ("the") in front of the root.  Each noun should be learned with its definite article which indicates its gender.  Second declension neuter nouns are marked by the definite article "τό ."  The stem of second declension nouns end with an omicron.

Greek nouns are [[u]]masculine[[/u]], [[u]]feminine[[/u]], or [[u]]neuter[[/u]] in gender.  Often this gender is more a syntactic feature than a metaphysical statement as many inanimate objects are given grammatic gender.  Thus "year" ( ἔτος ) is neuter while "day" ( ἡμέρα ) is feminine but "time" ( χρόνος ) is masculine.   Gender is indicated by the definite article marker.  It should be learned with the noun.
As in English, Greek has both [[u]]singular[[/u]] and [[u]]plural[[/u]] nouns.  The verb must match the number of the subject noun the same way as in English:

The students [[u]]love[[/u]] Greek.
The student [[u]]loves[[/u]] Greek.
There are 5 inflectional forms which mark the various cases or roles that nouns play in sentences.

items.label: Nominative form
items.text: :      marks the subject of the sentence.

content.text: [[u]]Music[[/u]] calms the heart.
"Music" is the subject of the sentence.  In Greek it would be marked with a nominative inflectional ending.
The Pharisee went to the house [[u]]of God[[/u]].
The Pharisee went to [[u]]God's[[/u]] house.
"Of God" or "God's" would be marked in Greek with a genitive inflectional ending.
He spoke a word [[u]]to the apostle[[/u]].
"To the apostle" would be marked with a dative inflectional ending in Greek.
The dative functions in many ways.  It may also be translated "with" or "in" in some contexts.

items.label: Accusative form
items.text: :       indicates the object of the sentence

content.text: Joy saw [[u]]the ball[[/u]].
"The ball" is the object of the sentence.  It would be marked by an accusative inflectional ending in Greek.
[[u]]Brother[[/u]], you are the man!
"Brother" is a direct address and would be marked by a vocative inflectional ending in Greek.

legend.label: Vocative
legend.text: = direct address (e.g. O words, tell us ...)

legend.label: Accusative
legend.text: = direct object of a sentence (e.g. He saw the temple.)

legend.label: Vocative
legend.text: = direct address (e.g. O temple, the place...)

meanings.closing: Note that in the neuter the Nominative, Accusative and Vocative form are always the same.

content.text: The order of words in a sentence in Greek is generally the same as in English (subject/verb/object).  Greek puts inflectional endings on nouns in order to mark their case.  This allows Greek to change the word order for various purposes.  For example, the subject may be placed after the verb and the object placed before the verb for emphasis while retaining the original meaning of the sentence.

A declension is a grouping of nouns that are inflected with a shared set of endings.  The difference in endings does not affect the translation between first, second and third declensions.  The second declension nouns are characterized by an "o" as the final letter of the stem.  They are largely masculine or neuter.  First declension nouns are characterized by an "η" or "α" and are mostly feminine.  Third declension nouns have stems that end in a consonant.

In contrast to English, which uses "a" as an indefinite article (e.g. "a book"),  Greek has no indefinite article.  Thus the Greek indefinite noun may be translated "book" or "a book."  Greek nouns are assumed to be indefinite unless marked by the definite article ("the").  For now simply be aware of the nominative form of the definite article which will indicate the gender of the noun being learned:
When you learn nouns you should remember which article goes with it as an indication of the noun's gender.
